blogs.title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
blogs.description: MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private…
blogs.content: content type Featured highlight Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio October 15, 2026 MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators. In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed. Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio. Muse Spark Open Decode Speed Context size of 8,192 tokens Figure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens. Higher is better. We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers. Running Large Language Models with MLX We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads. We evaluate three frontier-class models ( Table 1 ) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively). Model Total Parameters Active Parameters Native Precision Evaluation Precision Muse Spark Open 816B 42B BF16 NVFP4 Mistral Medium 3.5 128B 128B FP8 FP8 Qwen 3.8 27B 27B BF16 BF16 Table 1: Language models used in this post. Models ship in various precision formats; we evaluate Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 in their native precision, and Muse Spark Open in 4-bit (NVFP4) precision. Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark . For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line: mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes. Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3 , respectively. Inference Performance on a Single Mac Studio Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2 , we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra. Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2 ). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts. Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3 ), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s. TTFT Speedup Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×) Figure 2: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. The M5 Ultra GPU Neural Accelerator shines on compute-bound workloads. Decode Speedup Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×) Figure 3: Decode speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, and the M5 Ultra’s 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth (vs 819 GB/s on the M3 Ultra) is a key advantage. The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4 ): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment. Peak Power Consumption Context size of 65,536 tokens Figure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra. While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers. Pipelining Inference Across Two Mac Studio Computers Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5 ) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes. Splitting Large Models Across Multiple Computers Figure 5: MLX supports two approaches to splitting large models across multiple computers. With pipeline parallelization, a model is split across depth, while with tensor parallelization, a model is split across width. MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation . These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives ( jaccl , pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch , a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes: mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute). In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7 ) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged. It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6 ). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192 ) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk k k k , the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k + 1 k+1 k + 1 , so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization. TTFT Speedup Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×) Figure 6: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Splitting the context (here into 8,192-token chunks) lets MLX overlap computation across the two machines — hence the speedup at 65,536 but not 8,192. Decode Speedup Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×) Figure 7: Decode speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Pipeline parallelization leaves decode speed essentially unchanged. Tensor Parallelization for Faster Inference Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5 ) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl , is critical for this approach to yield any speedup. With MLX’s high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with: mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers. With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5. The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s — the two-cable value reported in Table 2 , the one-cable run being an additional experiment. TTFT Speedup Two or four Mac Studios with tensor parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×; Muse Spark Open: two-machine pipeline) 2 machines 4 machines Figure 8: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two or four M5 Ultras with tensor parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Muse Spark Open does not fit on a single machine, so its baseline is the two M5 Ultra pipeline configuration. Decode Speedup Two or four Mac Studios with tensor parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×; Muse Spark Open: two-machine pipeline) 2 machines 4 machines Figure 9: Decode speedup of two or four M5 Ultras with tensor parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Muse Spark Open does not fit on a single machine, so its baseline is the two M5 Ultra pipeline configuration. Time to First Token (seconds) Lower is better 8,192 tokens 65,536 tokens Model M3 Ultra M5 Ultra 2 M5 Pipeline 2 M5 Tensor 4 M5 Tensor Muse Spark Open — — 8.4 8.2 4.8 Mistral Medium 3.5 95.9 24.6 24.5 14.4 7.5 Qwen 3.8 18.2 4.1 4.1 3.1 1.7 Table 2: Time to first token (TTFT) in seconds for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Lower is better. We report a single M3 Ultra, a single M5 Ultra, two M5 Ultras (pipeline and tensor parallelization), and four M5 Ultras (tensor parallelization). Decode Speed (tokens per second) Higher is better 8,192 tokens 65,536 tokens Model M3 Ultra M5 Ultra 2 M5 Pipeline 2 M5 Tensor 4 M5 Tensor Muse Spark Open — — 15.74 24.99 36.73 Mistral Medium 3.5 4.95 7.70 7.70 13.69 23.37 Qwen 3.8 12.46 19.69 19.44 33.27 50.89 Table 3: Decode speed in tokens per second for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Higher is better. We report a single M3 Ultra, a single M5 Ultra, two M5 Ultras (pipeline and tensor parallelization), and four M5 Ultras (tensor parallelization). Decode speed was measured over 128 generated tokens following the context. Local Agentic AI on Mac Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with: mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080 As with mlx_lm.benchmark , the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode , which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server: { "$schema" : "https://opencode.ai/config.json" , "model" : "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4" , "provider" : { "mlx" : { "npm" : "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible" , "name" : "Local MLX" , "options" : { "baseURL" : "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1" } , "models" : { "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4" : { "name" : "Muse Spark Open 816B (MLX)" } } } } } Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach. Conclusion Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio. blogs.title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
blogs.description: Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy…
blogs.content: research area Methods and Algorithms content type paper published October 2026 Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents Authors Feiyu Gavin Zhu†**, Xiaoyu Zhu, Jiqi Yang, Rui Yang‡***, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Yancheng Wang, Xinke Deng, Jean Oh†, Reid Simmons†, Joerg Liebelt, Xiang Kong, Zhongyu Jiang View publication Copy Bibtex Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from the reasoning candidates based on their likelihoods given the current context, without an auxiliary task head. Using pre-specified reasoning traces enables parallel scoring, where teacher-forced prefilling computes token likelihoods concurrently within and across candidates using a shared context KV cache. We evaluated SSR on seven multimodal search benchmarks using 2B and 4B models. Across multiple reinforcement learning objectives and supervised fine-tuning, SSR delivers significant efficiency gains without sacrificing task performance. SSR achieves an average success rate competitive with leading search agents of the same scale, while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28–54%. † Carnegie Mellon University ‡ University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign ** Work partially done while at Apple *** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. Learning Structured Reasoning via Tractable Trajectory Control July 2, 2026 research area Computer Vision , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference ICML Large language models can exhibit emergent reasoning behaviors, often manifested as recurring lexical patterns (e.g., “wait,” indicating verification). However, complex reasoning trajectories remain sparse in unconstrained sampling, and standard RL often fails to guarantee the acquisition of diverse reasoning behaviors. We propose a systematic discovery and reinforcement of diverse reasoning patterns through structured reasoning, a paradigm that… Read more Interleaved Reasoning for Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning May 28, 2025 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Long chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances large language models’ (LLM) reasoning capabilities. However, the extensive reasoning traces lead to inefficiencies and an increased time-to-first-token (TTFT). We propose a novel training paradigm that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to guide reasoning LLMs to interleave thinking and answering for multi-hop questions. blogs.title: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
blogs.description: Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit…
blogs.content: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Tools, Platforms, Frameworks conference EMNLP content type paper published October 2026 Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures Authors Mingfei Zhang, Amit Surana, Ziauddin Majid, Chenxi Wang, Michael Xu View publication Copy Bibtex Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on ToolBench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross-category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt-oss-120b). We characterize a stub-hallucination failure mode (the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names) that acts as a double-edged sword: on simple queries PtR’s stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, yet on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs. We further analyze token overhead and show that PtR’s extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction—one that can be driven by a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtP’s top-1 retrieval score). Related readings and updates. ProTIP: Progressive Tool Retrieval Improves Planning December 20, 2023 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for complex multi-step planning tasks, where the Tool Retrieval (TR) step is crucial for achieving successful outcomes. Two prevalent approaches for TR are single-step retrieval, which utilizes the complete query, and sequential retrieval using Task Decomposition (TD), where a full query is segmented into discrete atomic subtasks. While single-step retrieval lacks the flexibility to handle… Read more Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation December 18, 2023 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Workshop at EACL This paper was accepted at the UncertaiNLP workshop at EACL 2024. Large language models (LLMs) have the remarkable ability to solve new tasks with just a few examples, but they need access to the right tools. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this problem by retrieving a list of relevant tools for a given task. However, RAG’s tool retrieval step requires all the required information to be explicitly present in the query. This is a… Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning. blogs.title: Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
blogs.author: Pengfei Tian, Maxwell L. Bileschi, Zoi Tsangalidou, Sukhdeep Singh, Lucy J. Colwell
blogs.description: Learn how Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize novel antimicrobial peptides in hours.
blogs.content: October 15, 2026 Science Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity Pengfei Tian, Maxwell L. Bileschi, Zoi Tsangalidou, Sukhdeep Singh and Lucy J. Colwell Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity Share New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier. Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences. This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation. Finding new antimicrobial peptides Rising antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance. The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin. Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they aren’t similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt , holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects. To bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model) , a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary “grammar” of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels. Overview of the ProtNLM pipeline translating raw amino acid sequences into natural-language biological annotations for unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries. The functional annotation scope of the system covers protein names, function comments, subcellular locations, and GO terms, in addition to keywords. Collaborative intelligence Scientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. Working in Antigravity, the researcher and AI agent begin by setting a focused biological goal: find and computationally validate novel AMPs in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae . During an interactive, multi-turn session the researcher steers the scientific strategy, deciding which questions to ask and what evidence to collect, while the agent handles the heavy lifting of cross-database orchestration, structural analysis, and literature synthesis. Slide 1 of 6 Navigating a vast search space: The agent queries the database and filters millions of entries down to a handful of candidates worthy of attention. Here, the agent finds a bacteriocin (Uniprot ID: A0A0U0D591 ) with a length of 97 amino acids from the Lactococcin 972 family. Validating the novelty of a finding: To verify the novelty of this discovery, the researcher guides the agent to interrogate the candidate against curated knowledge in Swiss-Prot via the EMBL-EBI NCBI-BLAST service and confirm this peptide has no meaningful sequence homolog among manually reviewed proteins. Reasoning over 3D protein structure: The researcher steers the analysis towards structural evidence. The agent retrieves the candidate’s 3D model from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, querying it against experimentally determined structures to identify remote homologs, and superimposing the models to assess similarity. Here, the structural evidence corroborates ProtNLM’s prediction by showing the candidate's fold closely matches an experimentally determined bacteriocin. The structure viewer in Antigravity allows this structural analysis to be seamlessly performed in one place. Reading the biological context around a gene: The agent looks beyond the molecule itself to its genomic neighborhood, reasoning over whether the surrounding machinery supports the AMP hypothesis. Inspecting the flanking genes, it spots a revealing pattern: our previously uncharacterized candidate sits at the upstream of a tightly coupled operon, just 6 base pairs ahead of a ABC transporter permease and its potential partner ATP-binding protein, alongside another annotated bacteriocin and an XRE transcriptional regulator. This provides strong contextual evidence that it is part of a working bacteriocin system. Building a mechanistic hypothesis from the literature : By reviewing the existing literature, the agent proposes how the molecule might act and what pathogens it might act on. In this case, existing evidence suggests a mechanism of action targeting bacterial cell division, and a predicted potency spectrum spanning several drug-resistant pathogens. Generating an experimental plan: Finally, the agent translates its in silico findings into an actionable bench protocol, spanning protein expression, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, target engagement, and in vitro toxicity testing, bridging the gap from computational prediction to wet-lab experiment. This step is already in motion: this candidate - along with several others discovered through the same pipeline - are now in wet-lab validation, where experimental results will provide the ultimate test of the agent's analysis. The candidate we uncover in this walkthrough represents a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence but it still requires wet lab validation. What makes this meaningful is how dramatically it lowers the barrier to everyday biological workflows, turning days of fragmented database triage into a single collaborative session. While this session focused on a narrow amino acid window in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae , researchers can take the conversation in any direction, such as layering in new filtering criteria, exploring different sequence lengths, or targeting other priority pathogens. By broadening the search from human commensals to environmental microbes and beyond, scientists can guide the agent across UniProt to discover novel AMP candidates at scale. A shared 3D canvas for interactive collaboration A protein's 3D structure can help us understand its biological function. Examining a candidate’s predicted fold in space is key. To provide this end-to-end workflow in a single workspace, we are introducing the Biomolecular Structure Viewer , a 3D visualization tool embedded directly into Antigravity. The researcher and agent work together over a shared visual state. As the agent retrieves structures from AlphaFold Database or the scientist’s own predictions, it can dynamically drive the viewer. For instance, it can highlight key functional regions to visually explain its hypotheses. Crucially, this awareness flows both ways: actions like highlighting specific residues or pinning notes directly onto a binding pocket are synchronised back to the agent. A researcher can simply mark a region of interest in 3D space and ask, for example, "How might this β-strand affect Lipid II binding?", allowing the agent to immediately reason over the exact structural context the scientist is looking at. Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. The Biomolecular Structure Viewer inside Antigravity showing the AlphaFold-predicted structure of the candidate bacteriocin, giving the researcher and agent a shared 3D canvas to inspect and annotate functional regions. Accelerating Scientific Discovery Historically, uncovering insights like those in the workflow demonstrated above required fragmented and specialised software: writing custom scripts to query databases, manually exporting files to 3D modelling programs, managing disconnected genomic tools and working with multiple experts to design the wet lab assays. Because wet-lab validation remains resource-intensive, narrowing the search space to only the highest-confidence leads upfront is critical. Using Google Antigravity allows researchers to navigate the vast biological search space efficiently while leveraging accurate protein function predictions from a domain-specific model. Google Antigravity executes this end-to-end scientific reasoning in one place. This allows scientists to spend more time evaluating high-quality hypotheses, running experiments in the lab and solving research challenges. blogs.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
blogs.author: Brenda Potts
blogs.description: Zero-knowledge proofs can verify computing results without rerunning workloads or exposing sensitive data. Magnetar helps bring them into the mainstream with support for standard programming languages, major speed gains, and quantum-resistant security:
blogs.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) .
